subject: religious-studies
title: Leibniz and the Principle of Sufficient Reason
welcome_lead: Enter the library of Hanover, where Leibniz seeks the sufficient reason for everything that exists.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on Leibniz's contingency argument and its critics.
final_note: Why is there something rather than nothing? Leibniz insists the question must have an answer.

concepts.def: Leibniz's principle that nothing happens without a reason why it is so rather than otherwise.
A being whose existence is possible but not necessary; it depends on something else.
A being whose existence is necessary in itself; its non-existence is impossible.
Leibniz's 1714 metaphysical treatise in which the contingency argument appears in compact form.
Russell's charge that Leibniz illegitimately extends a property of parts (having a cause) to the whole.
An existence or state of affairs that has no further explanation; Russell's preferred status for the universe.

walkthroughs.body_html:
In The Principles of Nature and Grace (1714) and Monadology (1714), Leibniz asks 'why is there something rather than nothing?'

The sufficient reason for the totality of contingent things cannot lie within the contingent series; it must be a necessary being existing outside the series, and this is God.

The PSR holds that for every fact F, there is a sufficient reason why F is the case. Applied to existence, this means that for every contingent thing, there is an explanation of its existence.

Critics like Peter van Inwagen argue that the PSR, in its strong form, may imply that all truths are necessary, an unacceptable consequence.

In the 1948 BBC debate, Bertrand Russell denied that the universe as a whole requires explanation: 'The universe is just there, and that's all.'

To argue from causes of parts to a cause of the whole is, Russell claims, a fallacy of composition; the universe could be a brute fact even if every event in it has a cause.

mcqs.q: What does the cosmological argument try to prove?
options: That the existence of the universe requires a first cause or necessary being — usually identified with God — to explain why anything exists at all.
The design argument proves evolution is false.
The cosmological argument proves who created life on Earth.
The cosmological argument proves the Big Bang happened.

mcqs.q: What does the teleological (design) argument claim?
options: The design argument proves evolution is false.
The design argument proves God created the world in seven days.
The ontological argument is the same as the cosmological argument.
Apparent purpose, order or complexity in the universe implies an intelligent designer — Paley's watchmaker analogy is the classic example.

mcqs.q: What is distinctive about the ontological argument?
options: The design argument proves evolution is false.
It tries to prove God's existence purely from the concept of God — a priori reasoning needing no empirical evidence about the world.
The ontological argument uses scientific evidence to prove God exists.
The ontological argument is the same as the cosmological argument.
